candidates.text: I turned it over and there was no envelope, no stamp, no postmark — only the ticket itself, lying between the gas bill and a leaflet for a window-cleaning service, as though it had always been part of the post. The date across the top was tomorrow's: the same weekday, the same month, thirty-one years and one day ahead of the summer I left. Route 47, out through the marshes where the herons stood in the reeds; the conductor had punched it without looking up, the way he did for everyone, and the paper had gone soft as cloth in my wallet, and I had kept it, God knows why, because by then the line was being cut and there would be no more tickets to keep. I held it up to the window. The ink was fresh — faintly warm, like something just off a press — and the fare at the bottom was a sum I had no way of imagining paying. Someone had posted it. That was the part I kept turning over. Not the date, not the route: the posting. Because the 47 no longer runs past the marshes; it stops at the ring road now, and has for years, and the man who could have sent it has been in the ground since the winter my mother died. So either someone had found the ticket and dated it forward out of kindness or malice, or the timetable had never really stopped running — and tomorrow there would be a bus, and a conductor who did not look up, and a seat by the window with the reeds going by on the left.

The ticket was a return, and it was the return half that had arrived: the outbound stub had been torn off along a perforation so fine it looked like a scar. Route 47, the old green-and-cream livery, the fare in pounds and pence, and in the box marked for the date, tomorrow's date, written in the same looping hand that had filled in the destination thirty years ago — my mother's, I realised, the same hand as the note she had left on the kitchen table the morning she went in to register at the hospital: *back by six, don't wait up.* She had never come back by six. She had, in fact, never come back at all, and I had spent one decade not waiting and one decade not not-waiting, and now here was the return half, postmarked today, dated tomorrow, as though the timetable had simply been holding it all this time, patient as a station clock, waiting for somebody to travel on it. I went down to the corner and looked at the stop. The shelter had been swapped for a glass one and the timetable case was empty, but the pole was still the same pole, and the tarmac still held the pale rectangle where the old shelter's concrete foot had stood, and I stood there a long while in the wind, holding a ticket for a journey that had been paid for before I was born.

The envelope was addressed to me in my own handwriting, which was the first thing that made me sit down. Inside was a single ticket, buff cardboard gone the colour of weak tea, the sort they stopped printing in 1994, and the date stamped across the top was tomorrow. Route 47, the Kirkstall–Bramley line, a service that had been cut the year before I was born. I turned it over and read the fare — eleven pounds, paid in coins — and the little punched hole at the top edge was still ragged, still raw-looking, as though the conductor's punch had only just gone through. Then I understood what the ticket was actually for, and my hands began to shake. It wasn't a ticket to ride the bus. It was a ticket to be on it. Thirty years ago I had bought a seat on a bus that ran tomorrow, and the bus was coming, and it was coming for me, and the only way to find out where it went was to stand at the stop with the ticket in my pocket and my coat buttoned and my name on the envelope in my own handwriting, waiting.

task.brief: A bus ticket bought thirty years ago arrives in the post, dated tomorrow. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the ticket forces a small concrete decision
the paragraph makes the elapsed thirty years felt without explaining them
the ending leaves the reader uneasy rather than resolved
task.reference_text: The envelope had been forwarded twice and the postmark was this morning's. Inside, the ticket was warm, as though it had been held, and the destination printed on it was the town she had left at nineteen without telling anyone she was going.
